content: Studies examining physical activity (PA) during early pregnancy have shown that overall physical activity is protective against the development of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) in 13 out of 17 studies. Evidence suggests that engaging in higher levels of physical activity (greater than 15 MET-hours per week) may reduce the risk of GDM, although the certainty of this evidence is very low due to limitations in study quality and consistency. A narrative synthesis of three cross-sectional studies (n=12,189) found that two studies reported no association between prenatal physical activity and GDM, while one study (n=11,450) indicated a decreased risk of GDM with moderate to high activity levels compared to low activity. Additional data from Oken (2006) showed no effect of light, moderate, or vigorous physical activity on GDM risk. Regarding gestational hypertension (GH) and preeclampsia (PE), two superiority trials (n=107) reported mixed results. Yeo (2008) found a lower incidence of GH in women randomized to a walking intervention compared to a stretching intervention, while McAuley (2005) reported no difference in GH cases between aerobic and muscular exercise groups. Among pregnant women with overweight or obesity, no significant difference in GH incidence was observed between physical activity intervention groups and controls across five randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Similarly, three cohort studies (n=76,260) found no consistent association between prenatal exercise and PE, although some data suggested lower odds of PE with higher levels of physical activity. For mental health outcomes, evidence on the impact of prenatal physical activity on depressive symptoms is mixed. One RCT (Satya Priya, 2013) found that yoga improved depressive symptoms compared to non-yoga antenatal exercises, while another RCT (Gustafsson, 2015) found no effect of prenatal exercise on depression severity. Four out of five cohort studies (n=5,060) reported a favorable effect of prenatal exercise on depressive symptoms, while one study found no association. Cross-sectional studies also indicated an inverse relationship between physical activity levels and prenatal depressive symptoms. In terms of fetal health outcomes, systematic reviews found no significant association between prenatal exercise and low birth weight (<2500 g) or small-for-gestational-age (SGA) infants among pregnant women with overweight or obesity. Similarly, no relationship was observed between prenatal exercise and large-for-gestational-age (LGA) infants or intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR). However, the quality of evidence for these outcomes is generally low to moderate due to study limitations, including high risk of bias and imprecision. Overall, while physical activity during pregnancy appears to have potential benefits for maternal and fetal health, the evidence is limited by methodological issues, including high risk of bias, inconsistency, and incomplete reporting in many studies. Further high-quality research is needed to clarify these associations.
